reference: The qualified libraries were sequenced on the MGISEQ-2000 platform (BGI Shenzhen, China).
answer: The Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencing platform with paired-end 150 bp cycles was used for metagenomic sequencing in this study, as well as the HiSeq 2500 Illumina sequencers. contexts: ['. Third-generation sequencing such as nanopore sequencing (ONT), promises to circumvent these dif- ﬁculties by providing longer reads (>3 kilobase pairs [kbp]). This technology has become popular in clinical metagenomics for rapid pathogen diagnosis12 and in human genomics research13. Long-read sequences can help bridge inter-genomic repeats and produce better de novo assembled genomes14. While the MinION platform from ONT has been used for metagenomic studies15, it cannot provide sufﬁcient sequencing depth and coverage to sequence the many hundreds of genomes present in the human gut microbiome. PromethION (ONT) can produce far greater numbers of sequences compared to either MinION or GridION, averaging four-ﬁve times more data per ﬂow cell and the capacity to run up to 48 ﬂow cells in parallel; this makes it suitable for metagenomics and microbiome studies', '. The quality of sequencing reads was controlled by FastQC v0.11.961 and followed by trimming and removal of human sequences with KneadData v0.7.2. Shotgun metagenomic data analysis Quality-ﬁltered metagenomes were taxonomically proﬁled using MetaPhlAn2 v2.2.0.63 Functional analysis was performed using HUMAnN2 v0.11.264 in the UniRef90 mode with default settings. Accordingly, we obtained the relative abundance proﬁles of intes- tinal microbial taxa, gene families and metabolic pathways for each metagenome. This resulted in 333,661,332 contigs longer than 200 bp, totalling 453.5 × 109 bp, with an average N50 of 12,460 bp (Supplementary Table 2). DAS Tool v.1.1.057 with option ‘-score_threshold 0’ was used to integrate MAGs pro- duced by the three tools. Contigs shorter than 1 kb were discarded. question: Assess the conflict of interest landscape of this study and discuss how it should affect interpretation of the results.
reference: The study was funded in part by AG1 (Athletic Greens International). Two of the authors — Trevor O. Kirby and Jeremy R. Townsend — are employees of Athletic Greens International, and both J.R.T. and T.N.Z. have received funding from dietary supplement companies for research, honoraria for speaking at conferences, and fees for writing articles and consulting. However, the authors disclosed that the funders had no role in the collection, analyses, or interpretation of questionnaire data, clinical safety markers, or adverse events. Readers should weigh these findings alongside independent replications, and the study design itself — double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled with pre-specified endpoints registered on clinicaltrials.gov — does partially mitigate these concerns.
